Case report
A 62-year-old man presented with a 4-day history of pro-
gressive involuntary jerk movements in his legs with
unsteadiness during walking. He denied other focal neu-
rologic or systemic symptoms.
He had a medical history of arterial hypertension, dia-
betes mellitus under insulin treatment, and mild renal
impairment. He also referred balance disorder for 2 years,
without vestibular impairment, (as evaluated by the oto-
laryngologist), and a single episode of trunk stiffening
lasted 1 month, about 6 years before, improved thanks to
physiotherapy.
Neurologic examination revealed inconstant rhythmic
spontaneous contraction of both gluteal muscles, condi-
tioning gait instability; these movements were absent dur-
ing sleeping, whereas they were exacerbated by voluntary
or passive contraction of the same muscles, deep tendon
reﬂexes evocation, tactile stimuli, emotional stress resem-
bling startle reaction. Cognition and cranial nerve exami-
nation were normal. Strength was preserved. Deep tendon
reﬂexes were diffusely reduced, whereas patellar reﬂexes
were brisk. Vibration sense was mildly decreased in lower
limbs. Coordination tests were normal. Gait was broad
based. The rest of the examination was normal.
Blood tests including blood count, liver function, glu-
cose, proteinogram, thyroid hormones, and complete uri-
nalysis were normal; we found mild increase of creatinine
(1.46 mg/dL) and creatine phosphokinase (273 U/L).
Patient was then initially treated with benzodiazepines
(clonazepam 1 mg 2 times a day).
Electromyography and nerve conduction studies showed
myoclonic activity of the paravertebral, gluteus medius,
and abductor muscles of the hip, lasting 50–60 ms and
alternating with similar activity in thigh adductor group of
muscles.
Basal electroencephalogram recording was normal.
Simultaneous encephalogram/electromyography recording
and jerk-locked back-averaging analysis excluded the epi-
leptic origin of the movements. Brain and spinal MRI were
normal.
Symptomatic therapy led to mild initial improvement of
symptoms, followed by new increase of involuntary
movements episodes, requiring new hospitalization.
Further exams revealed high serum anti-GAD antibodies
titer (10,000 U/mL). Type 1 diabetes-related autoantibod-
ies in the blood (islet cell, insulin, phosphatase-related IA-2
molecule, zinc transporter ZnT8) were negative, C peptide
level was mildly reduced (0.54 ng/mL, normal values
1.1–3.27), demonstrating that the patient did not have type
1 diabetes. Lumbar puncture showed CSF anti-GAD
autoantibodies elevation ( [1,000 U/mL); cerebrospinal

ﬂuid glucose, total protein amount, cell count, cytologic
examination were normal; oligoclonal bands were absent.
Whole body CT scan excluded solid neoplasms.
Patient was treated with a single cycle of intravenous
immunoglobulin infusion and then he started immunosup-
pressive therapy with azathioprine 50 mg 2 times a day.
Treatment was effective and well-tolerated, therefore
symptomatic treatment with clonazepam was reduced and
then completely stopped after 1 month. Clinical re-evalu-
ation made 5 and 10 months after the second hospitaliza-
tion, when the patient was still taking azathioprine, showed
complete disappearance of the involuntary movements.
Discussion
Antibodies directed against glutamic acid decarboxylase
(GAD) are present in many patients with stiff-person
syndrome and increasingly found in patients with other
symptoms indicative of central nervous system (CNS)
dysfunction, such as cerebellar ataxia [ 1–3]. Other CNS
disorders associated with GAD antibodies include pro-
gressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus
(PERM), limbic encephalitis, refractory epilepsy, abnormal
eye movements, and palatal myoclonus [ 4]. There are not
described cases of gluteal myoclonus associated with the
elevation of anti-GAD autoantibodies.
Here we report the case of a patient with acute onset
thigh myoclonus associated with elevated serum and CSF
anti-GAD antibodies levels. The setting of symptomatic
therapy at admission could have masked the typical SPS
electromyography ﬁnding of ‘‘continuous motor activity’’,
although neurophysiological testing of the thigh muscles
showed alternating myoclonic activity, that has already
been described in patient with anti-GAD positivity. We
excluded anti-GAD antibodies elevation linked to mis-
diagnosed insulin-dependent diabetes mellitus; the auto-
antibodies typically found in diabetes mellitus type 1 were
negative; furthermore, patient received oral hypoglycemic
agents without worsening of disease for several years.
Although we could expect that the patient had type 1 dia-
betes (GAD is also a major autoantigen in insulin-depen-
dent diabetes, and up to 35 % of SPS patients have
coexistent type 1 diabetes [ 5]), for the aforementioned
features we are more prone to consider this patient affected
by type 2 diabetes.
The majority of patients with stiff-person syndrome
present with oligoclonal IgG bands and an increased anti-
GAD-speciﬁc IgG index; in this case we found an isolated
CSF elevation of anti-GAD antibodies titer, with normal
blood–brain barrier permeability parameters, testifying
anyway an intrathecal antibody production against GAD
epitopes. The patient also showed a past anti-SSA and anti-
Jo1 positivity (untested on this occasion), in the absence of
any sign of other autoimmune diseases or organ involve-
ment, demonstrating anyway a propension to disimmunity.
Even though anti-amphiphysin antibodies were nega-
tive, we decided to rule out the presence of a malignancy,
because there have been reports of paraneoplastic neuro-
logic syndromes in patients who presented anti-GAD
antibodies; baseline total body CT scan was negative, but
the patient is now undergoing imaging follow-up.
Many patients with GAD-associated neurological dis-
orders respond to treatment with immunomodulating ther-
apies. In our patient IVIg therapy and azathioprine, in
combination with symptomatic intervention, effectively
helped control disease symptoms and course.
